State Bank of India||Tech Risk.answer:
• Cyber security risk from external and internal threats is mitigated through a robust Information Security and Cybersecurity Framework, periodic comprehensive security reviews, and a Next Generation Global Cyber SOC upgraded in 2020 per RBI guidelines (p.562, p.722, p.544).
• Data privacy and regulatory compliance risk is addressed by a dedicated Data Protection Officer, GDPR‑aligned privacy framework, and a comprehensive Privacy Policy complying with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (p.722).
• IT system failure and service disruption risk is managed via a Business Continuity and Operational Resilience (BC&OR) Plan that ensures uninterrupted ATMs, Net Banking, YONO and Mobile Banking services, supported by Disaster Recovery Plans and regular testing (p.119, p.396, p.713, p.723).
• Third‑party and outsourcing risk, especially for financial and IT services, is controlled through RBI‑mandated outsourcing assessments covering ten risk types, half‑yearly reviews by the Risk Management Committee, and continuity provisions in the Outsourcing and IT Sourcing Policies (p.119, p.723).
• Operational risk related to inadequate internal processes, people and systems, including IT failures, is mitigated by a stepwise Operational Risk Management process featuring Incident Reporting, Risk & Control Self‑Assessment, Key Risk Indicators monitoring, and Root Cause Analysis (p.119).
• Information security architecture and data governance frameworks safeguard critical information assets, ensuring integrity, confidentiality and regulatory compliance across next‑generation technology platforms, AI/ML models and digital infrastructure (p.544).
• The Board‑level IT Strategy Committee provides oversight of technology and information security matters, approving IT strategies, monitoring IT risk metrics and ensuring alignment of technology investments with strategic objectives (p.560).
• Periodic evaluation and review of firewall rules, deviation/exception procedures, and agile security review processes are employed to detect and remediate unauthorized access and intrusion attempts (p.562).
• Continuous monitoring, detection and response to cyber threats are performed by a centralized Security Operations Centre that informs stakeholders for remediation, containment and learning from incidents (p.562).
• Compliance with the RBI Cyber Security Framework (dated 02.06.2016) and ISO/ISMS certification ensures structured recovery during disruptions and systematic management of information security risks (p.560, p.562).

• Recurring R&D expenditure for FY 2025‑26 was Rs 92 crore, bringing total R&D spend to Rs 92 crore and representing 0.89 % of sales revenue (p.70).
• Recurring R&D expenditure for FY 2024‑25 was Rs 80 crore, with total R&D outlay of Rs 80 crore, equal to 0.86 % of sales revenue (p.70).
• Total expenses recorded under research and development for FY 2025‑26 amounted to Rs 101 crore, comprising employee benefit and other expense components (p.126).
• Approximately 700 scientists are deployed across four R&D centres and dedicated process development units, driving practical innovation in process design and green chemistry (p.12).
• Divi's R&D infrastructure consists of the Divi's Research Center (DRC) at Sanath Nagar, Hyderabad, and Process Development Service Centres (PDSCs) at manufacturing sites near Hyderabad and Visakhapatnam (p.48).
• The PDSCs handle end‑to‑end activities including process development, scale‑up, optimisation, impurity profiling, pilot studies, pre‑validation, validation batches and technology transfer to manufacturing units (p.48).
• The nutraceutical facility in Visakhapatnam is a globally recognised, technology‑driven unit producing high‑quality carotenoids, astaxanthin, lycopene, canthaxanthin, apocarotenal and vitamin ingredients (p.48).
• Divi's reports that no technology imports were made during the last three years, indicating wholly in‑house development (p.70).
• R&D and capital expenditure dedicated to specific technologies for environmental and social impact improvements accounted for 100 % of total R&D spend (p.33).
• Technology‑focused R&D investments represented 7.90 % of total capex in FY 2025‑26, delivering reductions of ~13,500 tCO₂e emissions, ~159,500 KL water conserved and ~8,290 GJ energy saved (p.33).
• Process innovation emphasis includes adoption of continuous flow chemistry, genotoxic risk management and resource‑efficient green chemistries to enhance competitiveness (p.47).
• Government initiatives such as Production‑Linked Incentive (PLI), Research Linked Incentives (RLI) and the Promotion of Research and Innovation in Pharma MedTech (PRIP) programme are cited as drivers of increased R&D intensity (p.47).
• Capital investment on energy‑conservation equipment and on‑site renewable energy generation amounted to Rs 17.90 crore during FY 2025‑26, reflecting technology adoption for sustainability (p.70).
• Divi's own R&D centres develop technologies and processes for active pharmaceutical ingredients and drug intermediates, which are subsequently implemented at its manufacturing facilities (p.70).
• The company highlights its portfolio of intellectual property, patents and proprietary technology as key drivers of innovation, though specific counts are not disclosed (p.14).
• R&D expenditure as a percentage of sales rose from 0.86 % in FY 2024‑25 to 0.89 % in FY 2025‑26, indicating a modest increase in R&D intensity (p.70).

• The company pursued greater automation in its manufacturing operations, coupled with expanded flow‑chemistry capabilities, to execute increasingly complex chemistries at commercial scale (p.10).

• Low‑tension capacitor panels equipped with Automatic Power Factor Controllers (APFC) were installed to enhance power‑factor correction and reduce electricity losses (p.41).
• Energy‑efficient technologies and replacement of high‑consumption equipment were implemented, delivering an estimated conservation of approximately 8,290 GJ of energy during the year (p.41).
• Dedicated solvent‑recovery stations were established to enable efficient reuse of solvents, supporting green‑chemistry objectives and reducing waste generation (p.41).
• Final wash and rinse water is recycled for initial rinse steps in production, lowering fresh‑water consumption and overall process waste (p.41).
• Process solid residues are supplied to cement plants for co‑incineration as fuel, turning waste streams into useful energy sources (p.41).
• Waste‑management initiatives, including the above measures, achieved a reduction of roughly 46 MT of plastic waste in the reporting period (p.41).
• Manufacturing automation, encompassing multi‑step synthesis, impurity management, backward integration, yield optimisation and solvent recovery, is highlighted as a core competitive moat for the nutraceutical segment (p.46).

• Divi's allocated over Rs 15 billion in FY 2025‑26 to capex programmes across its three manufacturing units, adding technology‑led capacity, strengthening sustainability footprint and building infrastructure aligned with its future growth roadmap (p.5).

• Divi's plans upcoming product launches and continued backward integration to support growth and strengthen competitiveness across key generic APIs, forming a core element of its forward‑looking technology roadmap (p.11).

• The company aims to build long‑term customer relationships through deep chemistry expertise, execution reliability and scientific collaboration, positioning these as strategic technology pillars for future growth (p.7).
• A Peptide Centre of Excellence is being leveraged to strengthen capabilities across chemistry, manufacturing and technology platforms for peptide‑based therapies, supporting future product pipelines (p.10).
• Divi's continues to pursue green‑chemistry initiatives—improving atom efficiency, reducing waste and enhancing solvent recovery and reuse—to embed sustainability into its future technology roadmap (p.10).

• Scope 3 GHG emissions are slated to fall by 35 % by FY 2034 and by 90 % by FY 2050, reflecting planned supply‑chain technology and decarbonisation actions (p.17).
• Process innovation priorities include continuous flow chemistry, genotoxic risk management and resource‑efficient green chemistries, which are identified as competitive advantages in the company’s future technology agenda (p.47).
• Divi's has recalibrated its 2030 sustainability targets under the Science Based Targets initiative, embedding measurable energy‑efficiency and emissions‑reduction goals into its forthcoming technology investments (p.17).

• DLF has migrated its core finance and operations to the SAP Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) platform, enabling integrated processes, automation and data‑driven decision‑making across the group (p.17, p.76).
• The company operates a digital complaint management system that logs customer issues, tracks them through defined stages and resolves them within set timeframes, enhancing accountability (p.69).

• DLF’s customer support portal on its website (https://www.dlf.in/customer‑Support) allows customers to raise queries and interact with the CRM team, forming a digital channel for service delivery (p.69).

• Sensor‑based low‑flow fixtures are installed throughout properties to automatically reduce water consumption, representing an IoT‑enabled sustainability measure (p.61).
• Rainwater harvesting systems are integrated at sites to capture runoff for groundwater recharge and reduce dependence on municipal supply, supporting sustainable water sourcing (p.61).
• Advanced wastewater treatment technologies are employed to treat sewage for non‑potable reuse (toilet flushing, irrigation, cooling towers, dust suppression), enabling zero‑liquid‑discharge compliance (p.61).
• Building Information Modeling (BIM) is utilized by project teams to improve construction management and design coordination, forming part of DLF’s technical capability framework (p.44).
• The ERP system is explicitly cited as supporting standardisation of processes and automation across business functions, reinforcing operational efficiency (p.76).
• Third‑party software is used by subsidiary restaurant and other businesses for accounting, though limitations prevent full SOC‑1 reporting, indicating reliance on external digital finance tools (p.237).
• Procurement and installation of energy‑efficient chillers and chiller pumps across rental properties have been undertaken to improve cooling efficiency and reduce operational energy consumption (p.51).
• ConstructionEd academy sessions delivered over 10,000 learning hours, reflecting extensive internal upskilling on construction‑tech tools such as BIM and MSP (p.44).

• The company installed an Internet of Things (IoT) based controller for chillers to enable live energy monitoring, enhancing operational efficiency (p.20).
• An occupancy‑based LED light sensor was deployed at DLF South Square to optimise lighting usage based on real‑time occupancy (p.20).
• A 350 kW electric‑vehicle (EV) charging station was installed at DLF Two Horizon Centre, Gurugram to support EV adoption and reduce carbon footprint (p.20).
• A conventional air blower in the STP at DLF South Square was replaced with a high‑energy‑efficient air blower, improving energy consumption (p.20).

• A high‑efficiency air blower replaced a conventional blower in the STP at DLF South Square, resulting in an annual electricity saving of 5,184 kWh (p.20).

• Approximately one‑third of terrace space at selected development sites is utilised for solar‑panel installations to generate clean energy (p.65).
• Rooftop solar installations with a cumulative capacity of about 5 MW have been deployed across DLF’s rental properties, contributing to renewable‑energy supply (p.65).
• DLF Cyber City, Hyderabad operates entirely on renewable electricity, demonstrating full‑scale adoption of green power (p.65).
• DLF Cyber City, Chennai sources 85 % of its power from green energy, showcasing a high proportion of renewable electricity usage (p.65).
• DLF Mall of India, Noida has achieved 50 % renewable‑energy integration, indicating significant on‑site clean‑energy generation (p.65).
• Select commercial assets utilise wind energy and open‑access solar power to diversify clean‑energy procurement and lower carbon intensity (p.65).
• Select retail properties have entered into Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) with third‑party solar providers to supplement renewable‑energy sourcing (p.65).
• Existing wind‑energy PPAs at select rental properties continue to contribute to the renewable‑energy mix, enhancing overall sustainability (p.65).

• Project delays and cost overruns caused by regulatory temporary halts on construction due to deteriorating environmental conditions, prompting the Company to conduct a comprehensive Climate Change Risk Assessment for its rental portfolio (p.46).
• Transition risk from the global shift to a low‑carbon economy forces DLF to adopt emerging technologies and sustainable energy solutions, which it is addressing through scenario‑based climate risk assessments and capital allocation for adaptation initiatives (p.46).
• Cyber security threats identified as a key operational risk are mitigated by deploying multi‑factor authentication, endpoint device security, disk encryption, data‑leakage prevention and continuous security log monitoring across its IT infrastructure (p.70).
• Migration from legacy accounting software revealed that the new system’s audit‑trail feature is not enabled for direct data changes under certain access rights, highlighting a gap in IT general controls that requires remediation (p.237).
• For FY 2024 the Group does not possess a SOC 1 Type 2 report, preventing confirmation that audit‑trail preservation complies with statutory requirements, a control deficiency flagged by auditors (p.237).
• Revenue recognition under Ind AS 115 involves significant judgement on performance obligations and transfer of control, a key audit matter that underscores reliance on robust contract‑management and IT systems (p.110).
• To curb reliance on conventional power, DLF installed Variable Frequency Drives on chilled‑water pumps and high‑efficiency air blowers, achieving annual electricity savings of 30,741 kWh and 5,184 kWh respectively (p.20).
• The report notes ongoing technology absorption initiatives but provides limited detail, suggesting potential skill or capability gaps in adopting new construction and energy‑efficiency technologies (p.20).
• Frequent changes in development guidelines, environmental clearances, taxation and zoning regulations create compliance‑related technology challenges, leading DLF to maintain robust monitoring and risk‑register processes (p.78).
• Internal audit observations on risk registers and control frameworks indicate a need to strengthen IT general controls and data integrity mechanisms across business units (p.78).

• The company’s IT infrastructure and information security management system are certified to ISO 27001, providing a globally recognised framework for data security and business continuity (p.147, p.202).
• A centralised 24 × 7 Cyber Security Operations Centre continuously monitors, detects, analyses and responds to cyber threats across enterprise systems, employing AI‑enabled security analytics for real‑time protection (p.147).
• The Cyber Security function leverages AI and machine‑learning driven threat detection to enhance proactive risk identification, behavioural analysis and automated mitigation of emerging threats (p.147).
• An OT security framework is implemented to safeguard critical operational infrastructure, ensuring continuity, safety and regulatory compliance for plant control systems (p.147).
• An Experience Centre has been established to enable benchmarking, capability development, cyber‑range simulations and security product testing, supporting in‑house capability building (p.147).
• The Application Security (AppSec) function integrates DevSecOps practices, including static and dynamic application security testing (SAST and DAST), to assess internally developed applications throughout the secure development lifecycle (p.147).
• Data Loss Prevention (DLP) controls are deployed as part of the in‑house application security suite to prevent unauthorised data exfiltration (p.147).
• The Information and Cybersecurity Strategy is underpinned by a robust governance framework and a technology‑enabled GRC platform that provides continuous risk identification, internal controls, autonomous audit and compliance validation (p.146).
• The company strengthens cyber resilience using AI/ML‑based predictive analytics, automation and adaptive security controls to counter sophisticated cyber threats (p.146).
• Advanced threat intelligence, continuous monitoring and a robust incident‑response capability are embedded to manage evolving cyber risk proactively (p.146).
• A Cybersecurity and Data Privacy policy is published on the corporate website, outlining the entity’s commitment to cyber‑security preparedness and data‑privacy protection (p.224).
• The company reports zero data‑breach incidents, with no instances of breaches involving personally identifiable information during the reporting period (p.224, p.162).
• Regular internal and external audits, including surveillance audits by accredited certification bodies, validate the integrity, resilience and ISO 27001:2022 compliance of the IT infrastructure (p.147).
• The Cybersecurity GRC team conducts internal audits to assess adherence to information security policies and controls, complemented by Management Audit and Assurance Services (MAAS) oversight (p.147).
• Continuous learning, simulated exercises, awareness campaigns and regular email updates embed a strong culture of cybersecurity, accountability and data privacy across the organisation (p.147).
• The Board’s Risk Management Committee has constituted sub‑committees focused on information technology and data security, providing governance oversight at the board level (p.160).
• Real‑time security monitoring is deployed across all layers—from end‑user devices to network, applications and data—enhancing detection and response capabilities (p.162).
• The company periodically reviews cyber‑security maturity, enhancing processes and technology controls in line with evolving threat scenarios (p.162).
• Standard operating procedures, policies and periodic internal and third‑party audits and tests are performed to assess resilience against hackers, malware and other cyber‑attacks (p.201).
• The Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) and Chief Information Officer (CIO) lead digitalisation and cybersecurity initiatives, overseeing implementation of systems, compliance monitoring and employee training across divisions (p.146).

NTPC Green Energy Ltd.||Technology Pain.answer:
• Cybersecurity and data‑breach risks are highlighted as potential disruptors to operations, prompting the company to implement cybersecurity controls, access‑management, data‑protection protocols, continuous system monitoring, employee awareness programmes and incident‑response mechanisms (p.94).
• Talent gaps and attrition in skilled employees for digital systems, SCADA, analytics and asset‑management are flagged as continuity risks, with the firm responding through structured training, career development, succession planning, employee engagement and competitive compensation initiatives (p.94).
• Auditors note a scope limitation in that no formal IT General Controls audit, penetration testing, or detailed cybersecurity/data‑integrity assessment was performed on NGEL’s SCADA or MIS systems, indicating a gap in comprehensive IT assurance (p.138).
• Technology‑related regulatory changes and evolving standards are identified as factors that could affect project economics and commissioning schedules, mitigated by leveraging the diversified portfolio, NTPC Group parentage, strong project‑management capabilities and heightened engagement with central/intermediary counterparties (p.43).
• Supply‑chain variability and dependence on critical equipment vendors are recognised as risks that may delay project timelines, addressed through rigorous due‑diligence, vendor assessments, diversification of suppliers and ongoing monitoring of critical components (p.95).
• The shift toward storage‑linked, hybrid and dispatchable renewable solutions increases project complexity and execution intensity, creating integration challenges that the company seeks to manage via its established project‑execution strengths and parent company support (p.43).
• Data‑quality concerns in SCADA‑derived information are mitigated by ensuring automated meter and generation readings are transmitted directly to a centralized MIS with minimal manual intervention, thereby reducing transcription risk (p.138).
• Potential delays in power‑sale agreement closures arising from evolving regulatory standards and technology‑related changes are mitigated by the company’s diversified asset base and proactive engagement with counterparties (p.43).
• Access to the centralized MIS is restricted to authorized personnel only, a control measure introduced to safeguard data integrity and limit unauthorized system access (p.138).
• The reliance on digital platforms and remote monitoring underscores the need for robust IT infrastructure, yet the absence of a full ITGC audit highlights a lingering vulnerability in system assurance (p.138).

JSW Steel Ltd.||Technology Pain Areas.answer:
• The company flagged manual inspection dependency as a critical pain point and mitigated it by deploying the Vision.AI Suite to automate inspection and defect visualisation, reducing reliance on human checks (p.49).
• Process variability was identified as a technology challenge; the firm addressed it by accelerating AI, Machine Learning and advanced process control systems across manufacturing to stabilise operations (p.49).
• Equipment reliability concerns were tackled through a Condition‑based Monitoring Programme deploying over 20,000 sensors, enabling predictive maintenance and real‑time asset monitoring (p.49, p.23).
• Decision‑making efficiency gaps were remedied by introducing AI‑assisted operator insights, automated anomaly detection and real‑time dashboards that accelerate management actions (p.49, p.48).
• Integration difficulty between IT and OT was recognised, prompting the strengthening of Digital‑IT‑OT convergence via an Enterprise Data Lake, the TEJAS Platform and enterprise‑wide IT‑OT integration initiatives (p.23, p.48).
• Data latency between field events and management response was a noted issue; the company built a private 5G network with 14 towers and a 10 Gbps fibre backbone to enable low‑latency IIoT data flows (p.49).
• The need for robust internal controls over technology was highlighted, leading to the implementation of comprehensive IT General Controls, an integrated ERP system and a continuous Information Security Policy (p.195).
• Audit scrutiny of complex tax and litigation exposures underscored the importance of accurate data governance, prompting the use of a Digital Scope of Work (SOW) system to enhance traceability and audit readiness (p.284).
• Legacy system integration risk was implied by the rollout of a platform‑led operating model that emphasizes seamless integration across plants and business units, reducing reliance on disparate legacy applications (p.48).
• Vendor dependency concerns were indirectly addressed by deploying a private 5G infrastructure and partnering with network equipment providers to ensure in‑house control over critical communications (p.49).

• The complexity of Airtel’s IT systems and the massive volume of data processed, especially for tariff‑plan updates, creates revenue‑recognition risk, leading auditors to test general IT controls, automated controls, interfaces and system‑generated reports (p.164, p.209).
• Frequent changes to tariff plans and high‑volume call‑data‑record processing risk billing inaccuracies, prompting detailed validation of CDRs against price masters and inter‑system reconciliations between billing and prepaid applications (p.164, p.209).
• Legacy equipment delays, spare‑part shortages, software errors and fiber‑cuts expose the network to technical failures, mitigated by operating advanced Network Operations Centers (NOCs) across India and Africa for real‑time monitoring and rapid fault resolution (p.30).
• Dependence on external partners and partner unavailability can disrupt service continuity; Airtel addresses this by shifting network planning in‑house to strengthen architectural control and improve long‑term reliability (p.30).
• Erratic last‑mile IT connectivity in certain geographies hampers service delivery, identified as a risk without a specific mitigation mentioned in the excerpts (p.30).
• Poor IT staff quality in developing markets leads to system failures and delayed recoveries, highlighting a skill‑shortage challenge for maintaining robust IT operations (p.30).
• Rapid technological shifts and evolving customer needs make timely adaptation a constant challenge, cited as a strategic pain point for the company (p.91).
• Monetisation of 5G investments remains subdued without compelling customer‑centric use cases, creating a revenue‑generation pain point for the network rollout (p.91).
• Exponential growth in data demand threatens high‑quality network experience, prompting Airtel to aggressively densify the network with small cells, Massive MIMO and new macro sites (p.32).
• To meet surging data demand, Airtel has enabled 5G Stand‑Alone on 100 % of sites, allowing concurrent 5G SA and NSA services and supporting higher spectral efficiency (p.32).
• Organizations slow to convert AI and generative‑AI experiments into large‑scale deployment risk losing relevance and margins, identified as a structural, time‑sensitive technology pain (p.32).
• Climate‑related physical and transition risks can degrade telecom infrastructure, increase O&M costs and threaten personnel safety; Airtel has conducted a comprehensive climate‑risk assessment and devised a climate‑proof plan that includes re‑engineering of infrastructure (p.32).
• Lack of digitisation and innovation is flagged as a strategic weakness, driving the need for accelerated digital transformation initiatives (p.32).
• High‑frequency software upgrades, patches and version changes create operational complexity, noted as a risk in the rapidly evolving systems landscape (p.30).
• Equipment failures, inadequate redundancy paths and weak disaster‑recovery mechanisms can adversely impact network availability, prompting investments in resilient infrastructure design (p.30).
• Energy or fuel shortages pose a risk to network operations, highlighted as a technology‑related vulnerability (p.30).
• Partner dependencies and partner unavailability are cited as risks that can affect service continuity, leading to increased focus on internal capability building (p.30).
• The need to continuously enhance network quality by addressing congestion, improving indoor coverage, reducing call drops and increasing data speeds is a persistent operational pain point (p.30).
• Climate‑change‑driven natural disasters can disrupt infrastructure and increase repair costs, prompting Airtel to incorporate flood‑prone area design criteria into its infrastructure planning (p.32).
• Rapid data‑traffic growth requires heavy investment in data‑capacity and broadband expansion, identified as a strategic technology pain that drives capital allocation decisions (p.32).
